condensationSequenceDial.title: The disk sorts its own solids
condensationSequenceDial.subtitle: Move a sampling point outward through a young disk and watch materials freeze out in order
condensationSequenceDial.aria: A temperature-against-radius plot of a protoplanetary disk with condensation thresholds marked
condensationSequenceDial.hintInside: Only {count} material classes have condensed here. A body assembling at this radius is built from rock and metal — dry, dense, and short of the solids a giant's core needs.
condensationSequenceDial.hintOutside: {count} material classes are available here. Past the water line the solid budget jumps several-fold and everything built out here is part ice — which is why giant cores form beyond this line and not inside it.

satelliteMassBudget.title: How large a moon a giant can grow
satelliteMassBudget.subtitle: Every satellite system in the Solar System lands near one ten-thousandth of its host's mass
satelliteMassBudget.aria: A log-log plot of satellite-to-host mass ratio against host mass, with the observed ceiling marked
satelliteMassBudget.subject: Pandora
satelliteMassBudget.requiredHost: For this moon to be an ordinary disk product, its host would have to weigh about {mass} Jupiters — past the roughly thirteen where a planet stops being a planet and starts burning deuterium.

disk.name: Grown in place
disk.hint: Moons condense from the gas and dust the giant funnels into its own orbit. This is how the Galilean moons formed, and it explains their tidy circular, coplanar orbits — but it caps their combined mass.
disk.cost: buys the regular orbits Pandora's siblings appear to have, but cannot deliver the mass

capture.name: Captured
capture.hint: The moon formed elsewhere as an independent world and was later trapped. Neptune did this to Triton. Nothing caps the mass, because the moon never grew from the giant's disk at all.
capture.cost: solves the mass outright, but capture normally leaves a tilted, stretched orbit that then needs a long time to settle

impact.name: Merged
impact.hint: Several ordinary disk-grown moons destabilised and collided, and the survivor is their merger. Earth's Moon came out of a collision like this, in reverse.
impact.cost: reaches the mass and melts the body enough to explain a differentiated interior, but requires a violent, well-timed accident

daisyworld.title: Daisyworld
daisyworld.subtitle: A planet that regulates its own temperature with no controller and no foresight
daisyworld.aria: A plot of planetary temperature against solar brightness: a living world's temperature stays nearly flat across a wide range while a bare lifeless world's temperature climbs straight through it
daisyworld.hintAlive: Slide the sun. Black daisies seize the cold early world and warm it; white daisies take the hot late world and cool it — and the planet's temperature barely moves while the bare-rock line climbs straight past. No daisy intends any of it.
daisyworld.hintDead: Past the daisies' limits the planet is bare rock again, and its temperature tracks the lifeless line exactly. The regulation only exists while life does.

habitableZone.title: The habitable zone
habitableZone.subtitle: Where liquid water can survive on a world's surface
habitableZone.hint: Drag the star's brightness and the distance to find the liquid-water band.

whittaker.title: Whittaker biome diagram
whittaker.subtitle: Temperature × rainfall decides which biome a climate grows
whittaker.hint: Drag the point — or use the sliders — to see which climate grows which biome. Pandora is warm and wet: rainforest runs wide.

circulationBands.title: Atmospheric circulation
circulationBands.subtitle: Spin rate sets the width of the Hadley cell
circulationBands.intro: The same law, two spin speeds. A slower spin weakens the Coriolis effect and widens the Hadley cell - so the equatorial rain belt swells and the deserts are pushed to high latitudes.
circulationBands.takeaway: The width of the cell sets the latitude of every forest and desert - and because Pandora spins slowly, its rainforest spreads across almost the whole world.

atmosphere.title: Atmosphere comparison
atmosphere.subtitle: The same oxygen push, a world of difference in CO₂ pressure
atmosphere.takeaway: The same oxygen push — but a world of difference in CO₂ pressure.

detectionScope.title: Detecting a world you cannot see
detectionScope.subtitle: Three windows onto the same orbiting planet
detectionScope.descRv: The planet tugs the star into a small wobble about their shared centre. As the star swings toward us then away, its light blue-shifts then red-shifts — a periodic wave that betrays a world we never see.
detectionScope.descTransit: When the planet crosses in front of the star, it blocks a sliver of light. The brightness dips and recovers on a clock — and the depth of the dip reveals the planet's size.
detectionScope.descImaging: Hide the star's glare behind a mask and you can photograph the faint dot of the planet beside it — the hardest method, but the one that truly sees a world.

eclipseClock.title: The daily eclipse clock
eclipseClock.subtitle: Polyphemus hangs fixed while the sun slides behind it
eclipseClock.hint: Drag time: Polyphemus hangs fixed in the sky while the sun slides behind it each late afternoon.

carbonateSilicate.title: The thermostat with no thermostat
carbonateSilicate.subtitle: How Earth stayed liquid under a sun 30% fainter
carbonateSilicate.co2Note: relative to today — high under a faint sun
carbonateSilicate.aria: Surface temperature against solar brightness: the regulated planet stays near liquid-water temperatures across the range while a bare rock scorches straight through.
carbonateSilicate.hintFaint: Under the faint young sun a bare rock would freeze solid — yet the thermostat lets CO₂ pile up, thickening the greenhouse until the planet stays liquid. This is why the early Earth never froze.
carbonateSilicate.hintBright: As the sun brightens, warmer rock in acid rain weathers faster, drawing CO₂ out of the air and thinning the greenhouse. The planet cools itself — the thermostat turning itself down with no one at the dial.

atmosphericDisequilibrium.title: Reading life off the air
atmosphericDisequilibrium.subtitle: A dead world settles; a living world is held impossible
atmosphericDisequilibrium.disequilibriumNote: reactive gases held coexisting — the biosignature
atmosphericDisequilibrium.deadPumpHint: Nothing to pump — the air has settled into chemical equilibrium
atmosphericDisequilibrium.aria: Atmospheric composition of the chosen world; the disequilibrium index reads {value}.
atmosphericDisequilibrium.hintDead: A dead world settles into chemical equilibrium — Mars and Venus are both more than 95% CO₂, inert and finished. There is nothing to pump and nothing out of balance, so a distant telescope reads: lifeless.
atmosphericDisequilibrium.hintAlive: Earth's air is impossible: reactive oxygen and methane coexisting, a mixture chemistry should erase. Only a ceaseless biological pump holds it open — and that disequilibrium, not any single gas, is the most robust signature of life we can read from afar.

exomoon.title: Exomoon Energy Balance
exomoon.hint: Balance the four energy sources to maintain a habitable climate on the exomoon. Too much heat boils the oceans, too little freezes them.

tidalHeating.title: Tidal Heating & Elliptical Flexing
tidalHeating.hint: Increase the eccentricity of the moon's orbit. The closer it sweeps to the giant, the more intense the gravitational squeeze, heating its core.

rocheLimit.title: Roche Limit Breakup Simulator
rocheLimit.hint: Drag the orbital radius slider. Inside the Roche Limit, the host planet's tidal forces overcome the moon's self-gravity, tearing it into a ring.

radialVelocity.title: Radial Velocity (Doppler Wobble)
radialVelocity.hint: Increase planet mass or decrease radius to make the star wobble. Note the wavelength shift: blue when approaching, red when receding.

directImaging.title: Direct Imaging & Coronagraph Mask
directImaging.hint: Without a coronagraph mask, the star's glare completely blinds us. Turn on the mask to block the star's light and reveal the planet.

alphaCentauri.title: Alpha Centauri Orrery
alphaCentauri.infoText: The Alpha Centauri system consists of three stars: Alpha Centauri A and B forming a close binary pair, and Proxima Centauri, a faint red dwarf orbiting the pair at a great distance.

transitTimingVariation.title: Transit Timing Variations (TTV)
transitTimingVariation.hint: TTV detects unseen planets. Toggle the companion planet to see the gravitational tug-of-war pull the main planet, making transits arrive early or late.

tidalLocking.title: Tidal Locking Simulator
tidalLocking.hint: Toggle between Unlocked and Locked. Unlocked moons spin freely; Locked moons are tidally distorted, keeping one face permanently turned toward the parent giant.

transmissionSpectroscopy.title: Transmission Spectroscopy
transmissionSpectroscopy.subtitle: Reading exoplanet atmosphere recipes by filtering starlight
transmissionSpectroscopy.hint: As a planet transits its host star, starlight filters through its thin atmospheric ring. Different gases absorb light at specific wavelengths, leaving characteristic 'dips' in the spectrum. Switch atmospheres to read their chemical recipes.

coriolisEffect.title: Coriolis Effect
coriolisEffect.subtitle: Sideways deflection on a spinning world
coriolisEffect.hint: Coriolis deflection is an apparent force resulting from planetary rotation. Choose a hemisphere, adjust the spin speed, and launch a probe. Watch the probe drift relative to the rotating surface, while moving in a straight line in space.

tidalHeatBudget.title: Pandora's tidal furnace
tidalHeatBudget.subtitle: How hard Polyphemus has to knead Pandora to keep it molten
tidalHeatBudget.aria: A log scale of surface heat flux with markers for the Moon, Earth, and Io; a movable needle shows where Pandora lands as eccentricity and mantle response change
tidalHeatBudget.hint: Slide the eccentricity and the mantle's dissipation response. Tidal power climbs with the square of eccentricity, so a tiny resonance-pumped e ≈ 0.001 already puts Pandora near a vigorous, still-habitable ~0.8 W/m² — about nine times Earth's heat flow.

heatSourceDecay.title: Three ways to stay hot
heatSourceDecay.subtitle: How a world's heat sources rise and fall over billions of years
heatSourceDecay.aria: Three curves over deep time: primordial heat and radiogenic heat both decline, while resonance-fed tidal heating stays roughly flat
heatSourceDecay.hint: Drag the age forward. The heat a world is born with leaks away and its radioactive fuel decays — so an ancient, small moon that is still molten must be topped up by a third source: tidal flexing, kept alive by an orbital resonance.

magmaEnergyLedger.title: Can magnetism melt a mantle?
magmaEnergyLedger.subtitle: The energy ledger that settles the 'magnetic heating' claim
magmaEnergyLedger.aria: A log-scale bar chart comparing tidal, radiogenic, and magnetic-induction heating power; induction is millions of times weaker
magmaEnergyLedger.hint: A static magnetic field does zero net work — its force is always sideways to a particle's motion. Only a changing field heats, through eddy currents, and for a rocky moon that power is five to seven orders of magnitude below tidal or radiogenic heat. Magnetism levitates Pandora's mountains; it cannot melt its rock.
